title: Cap. VII: Two modes of one sin's force — Calvin Rom. 5:12 against antecedent imputation
pass_a_gloss: Placeus insists the answer is serious and does meet the doubt. The claim that one man's one sin doomed the multitude admits two readings. Reading one (Garissoles's here): God immediately imputed that one sin to the whole multitude and doomed them for the imputed act. Reading two: the sin spread by natural contagion from one into all, multiplied, and so—because all had sinned—all were doomed. To keep readers from the first reading and from unworthy thoughts about God, Paul teaches the second: doom came because all sinned, not because only one did; each suffers for his own implanted sin transmitted from that one, not immediately for the single remote act. The ἐφ᾽ ᾧ wording itself hints at that transmission and touches sin no less than death. Placeus then cites Calvin's Romans 5:12 commentary—opponents who call Placeus novel must abandon Calvin. Calvin's order: sin first, death after. Some say we perish by Adam's sin with no fault of our own, as if he alone sinned for us; Placeus notes that that is almost a clear sketch of antecedent imputation, with soul-death (hereditary corruption) and bodily plus eternal death treated as proper punishments. But Paul states sin was propagated to all who bear its penalty, and presses the reason all Adam's line lies under death: we all sinned. That sinning means being corrupted and spoiled. The innate depravity brought from the womb is already sin before God and merits vengeance—original sin— even before it quickly yields fruit. Later Calvin lines: we all sinned because natural corruption fills us all; therefore inborn hereditary depravity is what is marked. Nothing could be clearer. Placeus is glad when the blow aimed at him also hits Calvin, and he grieves for the abandoned older teaching—or for those abandoning it. He flags again the new claim—injurious to God, in his view—that Adam's sin becomes everyone's only by imputation. Commonality is then blamed not on the sin's force, contagion, or natural spread, but on God, who by imputing chose to make common what otherwise would not be. Then our ruin would come from God making us sinners by turning another's sin into ours, with no reason except divine pleasure. Placeus asks whether a pious conscience is not stirred, recoiling, and horrified. Then: but let us proceed.
pass_b_english: The response does not play, but truly satisfies the doubt. For in two ways it could be understood that there was such force in one man's one sin that it should sentence the whole multitude of men to death: in one way, if it is supposed — which Doctor Garissoles does in this place — that God immediately imputed that one sin of one man to the whole multitude of men, and for that imputed sin sentenced it to death. In the other, if it is understood that that sin propagated and multiplied itself by a certain natural contagion from one man into all others, and so, since all have sinned, they were sentenced to death. The Apostle, lest the reader thinking the former way should suspect anything unworthy of God, teaches the latter, affirming that all men were sentenced to death not because one alone sinned, but because all have sinned; not immediately on account of one man's one sin, but on account of each man's own implanted in him, propagated from that one — which propagation is sufficiently hinted by the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, pertaining no less to sin than to death. Hear, I ask, most kindly reader, Calvin, from whose doctrine those who accuse us of innovated doctrine must of necessity withdraw — Commentary on Romans 5:12. Observe what order he sets here. For he says that sin preceded: from it death followed. For there are those who contend that we are so lost by Adam's sin as if we perished by no fault of our own, only because he had as it were sinned for us. (Antecedent imputation could scarcely be described more clearly than as that which death of the soul — that is, hereditary corruption — and death of the body and eternal death are thought to follow, as punishments properly so called.) And yet Paul expressly affirms that sin has been propagated to all who undergo its punishment. And then he presses that more closely when a little later he assigns the reason why all Adam's posterity lies under the empire of death. Namely, he says, because we have all sinned. Further, that 'to sin' is to be corrupted and spoiled. For that natural depravity which we bring from the mother's womb, even if it does not so quickly put forth its fruits, is yet sin before the Lord, and deserves his vengeance. And this is the sin which they call Original. And a little later: We have therefore all sinned, because we are all imbued with natural corruption. And again: It follows therefore that depravity inborn and hereditary in us is marked. Nothing could be said more clearly and expressly. Placeus congratulates himself when he sees Calvin struck through his side, and himself attacked together with him, and mourns the lot of the deserted ancient doctrine, or rather of those deserting it. Let it be noted here again the new doctrine — and, as it seems to me, injurious to God — that Adam's sin becomes common to all because of imputation. What therefore is common to all is to be ascribed not to the force or contagion or natural propagation of that sin, but to God, to whom it pleased by imputing to make common to all what otherwise would not have been common. Whence then our perdition, if not from God, who made us sinners by making another's sin ours? And why did he impute that sin to us, and make it ours, and us sinners? No cause is brought, or can be brought, except that it so pleased him. Is your conscience not stirred, pious reader? Does it not shrink from such a doctrine? Does it not shudder? But let us go on.
source_text: Non ludit, sed revera dubio satisfacit Responsio. Duobus enim modis in unius hominis uno peccato tantam vim fuisse, ut totam hominum multitudinem morti addiceret, intelligi poterat, uno, si ponatur, quod facit hoc loco D. G. Deum toti hominum multitudini unum illud unius hominis peccatum immediate imputasse, atque ob illud imputatum eam morti addixisse. Altero, si intelligatur, peccatum illud sese naturali quodam contagio, ab uno homine in alios omnes propagasse & multiplicasse, atque ita, quoniam omnes peccaverunt, morti addictos fuisse. Apostolus ne Lector priorem modum cogitans, indigne quicquam de Deo suspicaretur, posteriorem docet, affirmans omnes homines morti fuisse addictos, non quia unus tantum peccavit, sed quia omnes peccaverunt; non proxime ob unius unum peccatum, sed ob suum quisque sibi insitum, ab illo uno propagatum, quae propagatio vocibus ἐφ᾽ ᾧ ita, non minus ad peccatum quam ad mortem pertinentibus, satis innuitur. Audi, quaeso humanissime Lector, Calvinum, a cujus doctrina recedant necesse est qui nos innovatae doctrinae accusant, Comm. in Rom. 5. 12. Observa quem hic ponat ordinem. Peccatum enim praecessisse dicit: ex eo sequutam esse mortem. Sunt enim qui contendunt, nos ita peccato Adae esse perditos ac si nulla nostra culpa periremus, ideo tantum quasi ille nobis peccasset. (Vix potuit clarius imputatio antecedens describi, quam sequi putantur mors animae, id est, corruptio haereditaria, & mors corporis ac aeterna, tanquam poenae proprie dictae.) Atqui diserte affirmat Paulus, in omnes propagatum esse peccatum, qui ejus poenam luunt. Atque id deinde propius urget, quum rationem assignat paulo post, cur omnis Adae posteritas subjaceat mortis imperio. Nempe, inquit, quoniam omnes peccavimus. Porro istud peccare, est corruptos esse & vitiatos. Illa enim naturalis pravitas quam e matris utero afferimus, tametsi non ita cito fructus suos edit, peccatum tamen est coram Domino, & ejus ultionem meretur. Atque hoc est peccatum quod vocant Originale. Et paulo post, Peccavimus igitur omnes, quia naturali corruptione omnes imbuti sumus. Et iterum, Sequitur ergo pravitatem nobis ingenitam, & haereditariam notari. Nihil potuit dici clarius & disertius. Gratulatur sibi Placeus cum videt per latus suum peti Calvinum, seque cum eo pariter oppugnari, & desertae antiquae doctrinae, aut potius eam deserantium vices luget. Notetur hic rursus nova, &, ut mihi quidem videtur, Deo injuriosa doctrina, peccatum Adami propter imputationem commune fieri omnibus. Quod igitur commune est omnibus id non vi aut contagio aut naturali propagationi illius peccati ascribendum est, sed Deo, cui libuit imputando facere omnibus commune, quod alioqui commune non fuisset. Unde igitur nostra perditio, nisi ex Deo, qui nos fecit peccatores alienum peccatum efficiendo nostrum? Et cur peccatum illud nobis imputavit, & fecit nostrum, nosque peccatores? Nulla causa affertur, aut afferri potest, nisi quia ita ei libuit. Non excitatur conscientia tua, pie Lector? non refugit talem doctrinam? non exhorrescit? Sed pergamus.
